title: Grief becomes a verse
hook: Valmiki's grief at a hunter's arrow becomes the first shloka, and why Hindus carry verses by heart
carry: sacred verses are carried by heart

segments.voice: Yesterday, gita: one conversation, three roads. Your line was three roads to God: action, devotion, knowledge. Today, where a verse comes from, and where it lives.

A sage named Valmiki goes down to a river to bathe. On a branch nearby, two krauncha birds, a mated pair, are calling to each other. A hunter's arrow strikes one, and it falls; its mate cries out over it. Valmiki is overwhelmed, and words burst out of him, a curse on the hunter. But the words come out in an even rhythm, four lines of eight syllables, as if they'd been made to be sung. He walks back stunned by what he's said.
screen: `TWO BIRDS ON A BRANCH.` → `AN ARROW.` → `GRIEF COMES OUT IN RHYTHM.`

segments.voice: The Ramayana tells what happens next. Valmiki realizes his grief, shoka, has come out as verse, and he calls it shloka. Then Brahma, the creator, visits him and tells him to use this meter to tell the story of Rama. That's how, the tradition says, the Ramayana began: grief turned into verse. Valmiki is honored as the adi kavi, the first poet. The shloka became the meter of the great epics, and much of the Gita is in it too. Notice what it's built for: short lines with a beat, made to be chanted and remembered. For most of Hindu history, scripture lived less on the page than in the voice. The Vedas were passed down by memory, teacher to student, for centuries. In Hindi, a verse you know by heart is kanthastha: resting in the throat. That's today's teaching. In Hinduism, sacred words aren't only read. They're carried inside you, in sound, and said when they're needed: at a puja, before an exam, at a bedside. So here are a few candidates from these weeks. Two, forty-seven: your right is to the action, not its fruit. Six, five: lift yourself by yourself. Nine, twenty-six: a leaf, a flower, a fruit, some water, offered with love. Eighteen, sixty-six: come to me for refuge; do not grieve. Keep one that stayed with you, or any other. There's no correct list. Your own, even if imperfect, is better, as the Gita says of your own dharma.
screen: `SHOKA BECOMES SHLOKA.` · `VALMIKI, THE FIRST POET.` · `KANTHASTHA: HELD IN THE THROAT.` · `FOUR VERSES TO CHOOSE FROM.` · then, large: `KEEP ONE BY HEART.`

segments.voice: Choose your verse, just one. Say it softly, in Sanskrit if you know it, or in your own words. Say it again, slower, and notice where it sits: the throat, the chest. Say it a third time on the out-breath. That's how Hindu families have handed verses down for generations: not by reading, by saying, again and again.
Shloka, a verse. Born, the Ramayana says, from Valmiki's shoka, his grief; made to be held in the throat.
Your line: sacred verses are carried by heart. Valmiki's grief became the first one. That's day two hundred twenty-eight.

howItsDone: Many Hindus learn a few verses by heart, often from parents or grandparents, and recite them at puja and in hard moments; the Vedas were handed down orally for centuries, and children still learn Gita verses and whole chapters by heart.
